The deepest limit is that the past is gone and its record is fragmentary, so much of what happened is simply unknowable, and honest history acknowledges the gaps rather than papering over them with confident invention. Because interpretations are provisional, history is perpetually revised as new evidence surfaces, new questions are asked, and new perspectives are brought to bear, which is why each generation rewrites history in its own terms. This revisability is not a weakness or a scandal but the ordinary, healthy condition of a genuine field of knowledge, to be sharply distinguished from bad-faith denial of well-established facts. The mature reader of history therefore expects not final certainty but the best-supported account currently available, held with appropriate humility and always open to correction.

sections.heading: Memory, Public History, and the Uses of the Past
sections.body:
History as a scholarly discipline is only one of the ways societies relate to their past, and it lives in constant tension with collective memory, the shared, emotionally charged, and often mythologized understandings of the past that groups carry. The sociologist Maurice Halbwachs argued that memory is social, framed by the groups we belong to, and the French historian Pierre Nora explored the lieux de mémoire, the sites of memory (monuments, anniversaries, museums, symbols) through which nations sustain a sense of their past. History and memory are not the same: memory is felt, selective, and identity-forming, while academic history aims to be critical, evidence-based, and willing to unsettle cherished stories. Much public conflict over the past is really a clash between the two.

Because the past confers identity and legitimacy, it is endlessly put to use in the present, and history is therefore politically potent. Nations trace their origins to founding moments; regimes justify themselves by their version of events; movements draw inspiration or grievance from historical wrongs. This makes control over the past a prize worth fighting for, as George Orwell captured in his warning that who controls the past controls the future. Struggles over school curricula, statues and monuments, official apologies, commemorations, and the naming of atrocities are struggles over which account of the past a society will endorse, and historians are frequently drawn, willingly or not, into these public battles.

Beyond the academy lies the broad domain of public history, the practice of history for and with wider audiences through museums, archives, historic sites, documentaries, popular books, heritage tourism, genealogy, and, increasingly, film, television, and the internet. Public history reaches far more people than scholarly monographs and does vital work, but it also faces pressures, commercial, political, and emotional, that can pull toward simplification, nostalgia, or sensation. A recurring challenge is the gap between the messy, qualified findings of research and the clear, dramatic stories audiences crave, and part of the historian's public responsibility is to translate honestly across that gap without betraying the evidence.

Here it is vital to distinguish legitimate revision from its abuse. Genuine historical revisionism, the constant reinterpretation of the past in light of new evidence and questions, is the lifeblood of the discipline and a mark of its health. It must be sharply separated from denialism, the bad-faith rejection of well-established facts (most notoriously, denial of the Holocaust) in the service of an agenda, which is not history at all but its counterfeit. Recognizing the difference returns us to where this guide began: history is a disciplined, evidence-bound, self-critical, and revisable pursuit of understanding the human past. It connects onward to nearly every field, philosophy, politics, science, literature, memory, and identity, because to understand almost anything human is, in part, to understand how it came to be. Learning to think historically, weighing evidence, questioning sources, resisting easy myths, and holding conclusions provisionally, is among the most valuable habits of mind a person can acquire.

guides.title: How Historians Reconstruct the Past
guides.summary: An explanation of the methods historians use to turn surviving traces into knowledge of the past — the kinds of evidence, source criticism, dating, the auxiliary and scientific disciplines, the recovery of ordinary lives, interpretation and causation, and the debates that shape the field.

sections.heading: History, the Past, and Historiography
sections.body:
It is tempting to think that history simply is the past — the sum of everything that has ever happened. But historians draw a careful distinction between the past itself, which is gone and unrecoverable in its totality, and history, which is the disciplined study and reconstruction of that past on the basis of surviving evidence. The past comprised countless events, thoughts, and experiences that left no trace and can never be known. History is the far smaller, deliberately built body of knowledge that scholars assemble from the fragments that did survive, tested by method and argument. To understand how historians work is to understand how this reconstruction is done and why it is more than storytelling or opinion.

Because history is a reconstruction rather than a recording, it is always partial, always interpreted, and always open to revision. New evidence can surface, old evidence can be re-read, and questions that no one thought to ask can transform what we believe about a period. This does not make history arbitrary. Historians operate under real constraints: they must ground their claims in evidence, argue their case openly, and expose their reasoning to the criticism of other scholars. The discipline advances not by proof in the mathematical sense but by the accumulation of well-supported, peer-tested interpretations that command consensus until better ones replace them.

The study of how history itself is written and has changed over time is called historiography. Historiography reminds us that the histories we read are products of particular historians working in particular times, with their own questions, assumptions, and blind spots. A history of a war written in the nineteenth century, one written in the 1960s, and one written today will differ not only because more evidence has accumulated but because each generation asks new questions and brings new concerns — about class, gender, empire, environment, or ordinary life — to the same events. Reading historiographically means noticing these shifts and understanding that every historical account carries the fingerprints of its maker.

This guide surveys the craft that produces such accounts: the raw materials of evidence, the tests applied to them, the techniques of dating and specialised analysis, the ways historians recover the lives of people who left few records, and the acts of interpretation, explanation, and narrative that turn scattered facts into understanding. Throughout, two ideas recur. First, history is evidence-based: every serious claim must be answerable to something that survives from or bears witness to the past. Second, history is interpretive: the evidence never simply speaks for itself but must be questioned, weighed, and made to yield meaning by a thinking historian. Holding these two ideas together — rigour and interpretation — is the essence of the historian's method, and it is what separates disciplined history both from mere chronicle and from unfounded myth.

sections.heading: The Raw Material: Primary and Secondary Sources
sections.body:
The reconstruction of the past begins with sources, the surviving traces from which historians build knowledge. The most fundamental distinction historians draw among sources is between primary and secondary. A primary source is a piece of evidence produced during the period under study, by someone who witnessed or took part in the events, or an object that survives from that time: a letter, a law, a diary, a tax register, a photograph, a tool, a coin, a building, a recorded interview with a participant. A secondary source is a later account written by someone studying the period after the fact — a scholarly book or article, a textbook, a documentary — that interprets and synthesises primary evidence. Tertiary sources, such as encyclopedias and reference works, digest secondary scholarship into summaries.

This distinction is essential because primary sources are the raw material of historical argument, the closest a historian can get to the past, while secondary sources are the conversation among scholars about what that material means. A historian who wishes to make an original claim must return to primary sources; a reader who wishes to learn the current understanding of a topic turns first to good secondary works. Serious history depends on the disciplined use of primary evidence, tested and interpreted, rather than on the mere repetition of what earlier writers have said.

Crucially, the categories are not fixed properties of a document but depend on the question being asked. A history textbook from 1950 is a secondary source about the events it describes, but it is a primary source for the study of how history was taught and understood in 1950. A propaganda poster is a primary source both for the events it concerns and, even more reliably, for the attitudes and techniques of those who made it. What makes a source primary or secondary is its relationship to the historian's specific inquiry, not its form.

Primary sources also vary enormously in their intended audience and purpose, which shapes how they must be read. Some were meant to be public and official, such as laws, treaties, and monuments; others were private, such as personal letters and diaries never meant for outside eyes; still others were routine administrative records — censuses, ship manifests, court rolls, parish registers — created for bureaucratic purposes with no thought of posterity. These unglamorous records are often the most valuable of all, precisely because their makers had no motive to shape a story for later readers and because they can reveal, in aggregate, the lives of ordinary people who left no memoirs.

Understanding this landscape of sources — primary versus secondary, public versus private, deliberate versus incidental — is the first skill of the historian. Every subsequent method, from source criticism to dating to interpretation, is applied to this raw material, and the quality of any history depends first on the quality, quantity, and honest handling of the sources beneath it.

sections.heading: The Many Kinds of Evidence
sections.body:
The traces of the past come in far more forms than the written document, and part of the historian's craft is knowing where evidence can be found and how each kind must be handled. Written sources are the most familiar and, for literate societies, often the richest. They range from the deliberately narrative — chronicles, annals, histories, memoirs, letters — to the functional and administrative: charters, laws, treaties, tax rolls, census returns, court proceedings, wills, account books, parish registers, and, in modern times, newspapers, government files, and the vast digital record. Each genre has its own conventions and its own reliability, and a historian must read a legal charter differently from a private diary.

Material evidence is the domain shared with archaeology: the physical remains of human activity. Tools, weapons, pottery, coins, jewellery, clothing, food remains, human and animal bones, and the ruins of houses, temples, fortifications, roads, and whole settlements all testify to how people lived, worked, ate, fought, and died. For the long stretches of the human past before writing, and for the many people within literate societies who left no written trace, material evidence is often the only witness we have, which is why archaeology and history are close partners.

Visual and cartographic sources form another category: paintings, sculptures, engravings, and, from the nineteenth century, photographs and film, together with maps and plans. Images can record appearances, events, and attitudes, but they are shaped by the conventions of art and the intentions of their makers, so a medieval illumination or a propaganda painting must be read as an interpretation, not a photograph. Maps reveal not only geography but how people understood and claimed space.

Oral sources — spoken testimony, interviews, songs, poems, genealogies, and the transmitted traditions of communities — carry the memory of participants and, in societies without writing, the accumulated record of generations. They are precious for capturing perspectives that written records omit, though memory's fallibility and the reshaping of traditions over time demand careful handling.

Finally, the natural and scientific record increasingly counts as historical evidence: tree rings, ice cores, pollen preserved in sediments, isotopes locked in bones and teeth, and ancient DNA can reveal climate, diet, disease, migration, and kinship, letting historians reconstruct aspects of the past that no human recorded at all.

The skilled historian draws on all these kinds of evidence, matching source to question and combining them so that each compensates for the weaknesses of the others. A study of an ancient city might weave together its ruins and artefacts, its inscriptions and coins, the accounts of later writers, and the environmental record of its surroundings. This deliberate breadth — the refusal to rely on any single type of source — is one of the hallmarks of good historical work and one of the main ways that history's reach has expanded over the past century.

sections.heading: Source Criticism: Testing the Evidence
sections.body:
A source is not a fact; it is a claim, or a trace, that must be tested before it can support historical conclusions. The disciplined interrogation of sources is called source criticism, and it is the methodological heart of the historian's craft. It was given its rigorous modern form in the nineteenth century, above all by the German historian Leopold von Ranke, who insisted that history be founded on the critical study of primary documents and famously said the historian's task was to show the past wie es eigentlich gewesen — how it essentially was. His seminar method trained historians to scrutinise sources systematically rather than to trust received narratives.

Source criticism is traditionally divided into two stages. The first, external criticism, asks whether a source is authentic and what exactly it is: is this document genuine or a forgery, is it the original or a later copy, when and where was it produced, in what language and by what materials, and who actually made it? Answering these questions may require examining the physical object — the parchment, ink, paper, handwriting, seals, or, for material objects, the composition and manufacture — and tracing its provenance, the chain of custody by which it has come down to us. Forgeries, interpolations, and misattributions are real dangers, and famous documents have been exposed as fakes by such analysis; conversely, establishing a source's genuineness and origin is the precondition for using it at all.

The second stage, internal criticism, asks what the source means and how far it can be trusted as evidence for its content. Here the historian probes the maker's identity, purpose, and situation: Who wrote this, for whom, and why? Was the author a direct witness or reporting at second hand? How much time separated the event from the record? What did the author stand to gain or lose, what biases or loyalties shaped the account, and what did the intended audience expect? A partisan chronicle, an official propaganda piece, and a private letter each distort in characteristic ways, and the historian must read through the distortion to the reality behind it, while also recognising that the distortion itself is evidence of attitudes and interests.

Internal criticism also weighs plausibility and consistency: Does the source contradict itself or well-established facts? Are its claims physically and chronologically possible? Does it confuse events, exaggerate numbers, or repeat legend? None of this means discarding flawed sources, for nearly every source is flawed in some way; it means using each source for what it can reliably tell us and remaining alert to what it cannot.

The practical upshot is a habit of mind: never take a source at face value, always ask where it came from and why, and treat every document as a witness to be cross-examined rather than a verdict to be accepted. This critical stance, applied consistently, is what turns a heap of surviving texts and objects into trustworthy historical knowledge.

sections.heading: Corroboration and Weighing Conflicting Accounts
sections.body:
No single source, however carefully criticised, is usually enough to establish a historical fact with confidence, and sources frequently disagree. The historian's response is corroboration, sometimes called triangulation: the practice of testing claims against multiple independent sources and weighing them against one another. When several sources that could not have simply copied one another converge on the same point, confidence rises; when they diverge, the historian must explain the discrepancy rather than merely pick a favourite. Much of the real work of history lies in this patient reconciliation and adjudication of imperfect, competing testimony.

Independence is the key word. Two accounts that agree because one is derived from the other provide no more assurance than the original alone; genuine corroboration comes from sources that arose separately, ideally of different types — a written account confirmed by an inscription, an archaeological find, or an administrative record. A besieged city's fall attested by the victors' monument, the losers' lament, a neighbour's chronicle, and the burnt layer in its ruins is far more securely known than one reported by a single chronicler. Historians therefore prize the meeting of different kinds of evidence and are wary of long chains of texts that all ultimately trace to one source.

When sources conflict, the historian does not simply average them or trust the majority. Instead each account is weighed by the criteria of source criticism: which author was better placed to know, closer to the event, less motivated to distort, more consistent with independent evidence? A well-informed but hostile witness and a sympathetic but distant one may each contribute part of the truth. Sometimes the historian can reconstruct what probably happened by identifying the point on which even opposed sources agree, or by recognising a shared underlying event beneath divergent interpretations of it. Sometimes the honest conclusion is that the evidence does not permit a firm answer, and saying so clearly is itself a mark of good history.

Discrepancies are not only obstacles but clues. Why do two accounts differ? The reasons — differing vantage points, interests, later legend-making, translation errors, deliberate propaganda — are themselves historically revealing, exposing the concerns and conflicts of the people who produced the records. A careful analysis of why sources disagree can illuminate a period as much as agreement on the bare facts does.

Throughout, the historian must guard against the temptation to select only the evidence that fits a preferred conclusion, a fault known as cherry-picking. Intellectual honesty requires confronting the sources that complicate one's argument, not just those that support it, and adjusting the interpretation to fit the whole body of evidence. The strength of a historical claim rests not on any one striking document but on how well it accounts for all the relevant, independently corroborated evidence, including the awkward parts. This disciplined weighing of many voices, no one of them decisive alone, is how history moves from isolated testimony toward reliable understanding.

sections.heading: Chronology: Placing Events in Time
sections.body:
History is, among other things, the study of change over time, so establishing when things happened — and in what order — is fundamental. This task, called chronology, is more difficult than it first appears, because the past has come down to us in a tangle of different calendars, dating systems, and undated remains, and getting the sequence wrong can wreck an interpretation entirely. Historians distinguish between relative dating, which establishes the order of events without fixing exact dates, and absolute dating, which assigns a specific point on a calendar.

Relative dating is often the historian's and archaeologist's starting point. In archaeology, the principle of stratigraphy holds that in an undisturbed site, deeper layers were deposited earlier than those above them, so the sequence of layers gives a relative order. Typology and seriation arrange artefacts or styles — pottery shapes, coin designs, handwriting, architectural forms — into developmental sequences, allowing objects to be placed earlier or later relative to one another. In documents, internal references, the people and events mentioned, and the style of language can fix a text's position in a sequence even when it bears no date.

Absolute dating fixes events to a calendar, but calendars themselves are a historical problem. Different societies counted years from different starting points and by different systems: regnal years reckoned from a ruler's accession, eras such as the founding of a city or a religious epoch, and lunar, solar, or lunisolar calendars that do not map neatly onto one another. The widely used system of counting years before and after a fixed epoch, and the shift from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar in the modern era, both create pitfalls of conversion that historians must handle with care, since a careless translation between systems can misdate an event by days, years, or centuries.

To build absolute chronologies, historians exploit fixed points that can be tied to a known date — a dated inscription, an eclipse recorded in an ancient text and calculable by astronomy, a coin bearing a datable ruler's name — and then anchor relative sequences to them. Astronomical events are especially valuable because they can be computed backward with precision, so a battle described as occurring during an eclipse can sometimes be dated to the day.

Scientific dating methods, discussed more fully later, have transformed chronology by providing absolute dates independent of written records, allowing the deep human past to be placed in time for the first time. Yet even these come with margins of error that must be honestly stated.

The discipline of chronology thus underlies all historical narrative. Before a historian can explain why something happened or trace how one development led to another, the events must be correctly ordered and dated. Mistakes in sequence produce false causation — imagining that one event caused another when it actually came afterward — so the unglamorous work of getting the timeline right is a precondition for every larger interpretive claim the historian will make.

sections.heading: The Auxiliary Sciences of History
sections.body:
To extract reliable information from the strange and difficult objects that survive from the past, historians rely on a family of specialised disciplines known as the auxiliary or ancillary sciences of history. Each provides the technical expertise needed to read a particular kind of source, and together they form much of the practical toolkit of the working historian, especially for periods far removed from our own.

Palaeography is the study of old handwriting. Scripts change over centuries and vary by region and purpose, and a medieval charter or an ancient papyrus can be unreadable without training in the letter forms, abbreviations, and conventions of its time and place. Closely related is codicology, the study of the manuscript book as a physical object — its parchment or paper, gatherings, binding, and layout — which can reveal when, where, and how a text was produced and copied. Diplomatics, founded as a formal discipline by the Benedictine scholar Jean Mabillon in the seventeenth century, is the critical study of the form and formulae of official documents, developed originally to distinguish genuine charters from forgeries by analysing their structure, language, seals, and modes of authentication.

Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions carved or written on durable materials such as stone, metal, and clay. Inscriptions — on monuments, tombs, coins, boundary markers, and public decrees — are often the most direct surviving voice of ancient societies, and epigraphers specialise in reading, restoring, and dating them. Numismatics, the study of coins and money, is invaluable because coins carry dates, rulers' names and images, and political messages, circulate widely, and turn up in datable archaeological contexts, making them powerful tools for both chronology and economic history. Sigillography, or sphragistics, studies the seals used to authenticate documents, while heraldry deciphers the coats of arms that identify families and institutions.

Other members of this family include chronology itself, treated as a technical science of calendars and dating; genealogy, the reconstruction of family descent; and prosopography, the collective biography of groups of people — all the members of a senate, a guild, or a bureaucracy — assembled from scattered records to reveal patterns of power, kinship, and career that no individual biography would show. Philology, the rigorous study of language and texts, underlies the editing of ancient and medieval writings, reconstructing the most accurate possible version of a work from divergent surviving copies.

Archaeology, though now a large discipline in its own right, remains the great auxiliary science for recovering the material past, and it in turn draws on many laboratory sciences. The historian rarely masters all of these specialisms but must know what each can do and when to call on its expertise. This division of technical labour is what allows the raw, cryptic survivals of the past — a worn inscription, a faded charter, a hoard of coins — to be turned into legible, datable, trustworthy evidence for the larger work of historical reconstruction.

sections.heading: Bringing Science to the Past
sections.body:
Over the past century, and with accelerating force in recent decades, the natural sciences have given historians and archaeologists powerful new ways to interrogate the past, often yielding information that no human being ever recorded. These scientific methods have extended history's reach deep into prehistory and have settled, or reopened, many long-standing questions. The most famous is radiocarbon dating, developed by the American chemist Willard Libby in the late 1940s, for which he received the Nobel Prize. It measures the decay of the radioactive isotope carbon-14, which living things absorb and which then diminishes at a known rate after death, with a half-life of about 5,730 years, allowing organic materials such as wood, bone, and cloth to be dated up to roughly fifty thousand years old, within a calculable margin of error.

Dendrochronology, the study of tree rings, provides another absolute chronology. Because trees lay down one ring per year and the pattern of thick and thin rings reflects yearly climate, overlapping sequences from living and ancient timbers can be matched into continuous records stretching back thousands of years, dating wooden objects and buildings to the exact year and helping to calibrate radiocarbon dates. For far older geological and early human timescales, methods such as potassium-argon dating and thermoluminescence extend absolute dating back millions of years.

Beyond dating, scientific analysis reconstructs how people lived. The chemical isotopes locked in ancient bones and teeth record diet and, through elements absorbed from local water and rock, the geography of where a person grew up, revealing migration and mobility. The analysis of ancient DNA extracted from skeletons has revolutionised the study of prehistoric population movements, kinship, disease, and the domestication of plants and animals, allowing historians to trace the spread of peoples and pathogens across continents. Palynology, the study of preserved pollen, reconstructs past vegetation, agriculture, and climate, while ice cores and lake sediments provide detailed records of ancient climate and environmental change that illuminate famines, plagues, and the rise and fall of societies.

Remote sensing has transformed the discovery of sites. Aerial and satellite photography, and especially LiDAR, which uses laser pulses to map the ground surface beneath vegetation, have revealed lost cities, field systems, and roads invisible from the ground, rewriting the histories of regions from Central America to Southeast Asia. Ground-penetrating radar and other geophysical techniques let archaeologists map buried structures without excavation.

These methods are immensely powerful, but they are not infallible oracles. Each has assumptions, limitations, and margins of error; radiocarbon dates require calibration, isotope and DNA results demand cautious interpretation, and scientific findings must be integrated with, not substituted for, the traditional evidence of texts and material culture. The best historical work marries scientific data to documentary and archaeological analysis, letting each check and enrich the other, so that the past is reconstructed from every available kind of witness.

sections.heading: Recovering the Voiceless: Oral History and Material Culture
sections.body:
For most of the human past, and for most of the people in any society, the written record is thin, biased toward the powerful and literate, or absent altogether. Kings, priests, and officials left documents; the enslaved, the poor, women, peasants, and the inhabitants of non-literate societies usually did not. A history built only from written elite sources would therefore be a history of a small minority. Much of the most important development in the discipline over the past several generations has been the search for methods to recover the lives and perspectives of the great majority who left few or no written traces.

One key method is oral history: the systematic recording and analysis of the spoken testimony of living witnesses. Since the mid-twentieth century, historians have interviewed workers, soldiers, migrants, survivors, and ordinary people whose experiences never entered official archives, capturing memory before it is lost. Oral history is precious for giving voice to the marginalised and for recording feeling and everyday texture that documents omit, but it demands careful handling, because memory is selective, reshaped by later events, and shaped by the interview itself; the historian must weigh it as critically as any written source. In societies without writing, oral tradition — genealogies, epics, and transmitted communal memory — can preserve the past across centuries, as the historian Jan Vansina argued in his influential work on African oral tradition as a genuine historical source, though its transformations over time must be understood.

Material culture is the other great avenue to the voiceless. The objects people made and used — their houses, tools, cooking pots, clothing, and refuse — testify directly to how they lived, regardless of whether they could write. Archaeology of the everyday, the study of ordinary settlements, food remains, and household goods, reconstructs the diet, labour, health, and domestic life of people who appear in no chronicle. Even the human body, through the study of bones and teeth, reveals nutrition, disease, physical labour, and violence.

These methods have underpinned whole movements within history. History from below, associated with historians such as E. P. Thompson, deliberately shifts attention from rulers to the experience of ordinary working people, reading elite records against the grain to find the lives of the governed. Microhistory, exemplified by Carlo Ginzburg's study of a sixteenth-century miller's beliefs reconstructed from his inquisition records, examines a single obscure individual or village in intense detail to illuminate the mental world of ordinary people. Studies of enslaved and colonised peoples have developed ingenious techniques for reading the records of oppressors to recover the agency of the oppressed.

Together, oral history and the study of material culture, combined with the imaginative re-reading of conventional sources, have vastly widened history's scope, turning it from a chronicle of the powerful into an attempt to understand whole societies. This democratization of the historical subject is one of the discipline's greatest achievements and a continuing frontier of method.

sections.heading: Interpretation, Causation, and Narrative
sections.body:
Once sources have been gathered, criticised, corroborated, and dated, the historian faces the deeper task that distinguishes history from mere compilation: making sense of the evidence. Facts, the philosopher and historian E. H. Carr argued in his classic reflection What Is History?, do not speak for themselves; the historian selects them, arranges them, and interprets them, so that history is a continuous dialogue between the historian and the evidence, between present questions and past traces. The same body of sources can support different, though not unlimited, interpretations, and interpretation is where the historian's judgement, argument, and creativity come most fully into play.

A central interpretive problem is causation: explaining why things happened. Historical events almost never have a single cause; they arise from a tangle of long-term structural conditions, medium-term developments, and short-term triggers, from impersonal forces such as economics, climate, and demography, and from the choices of individuals. Historians debate how to weigh these, distinguishing, for example, the underlying causes of a war from its immediate occasion. They also wrestle with contingency — the role of accident and of paths not taken — against deterministic explanations that see outcomes as inevitable. Counterfactual reasoning, asking what might have happened had some factor differed, is sometimes used to test the importance of a cause, though many historians regard it as speculative and treat it with caution.

Explanation in history is not like prediction in physics. History cannot run controlled experiments or rerun events, and its generalisations are provisional and context-bound. The historian R. G. Collingwood argued that understanding a past action requires re-enacting in one's own mind the thought behind it — grasping how a situation looked to the people who acted, their intentions and reasoning — so that historical explanation is partly an act of disciplined empathy, recovering the logic of past agents rather than judging them by present standards.

History is also written, and its form is not neutral. To turn analysis into a coherent account, the historian must construct a narrative, choosing where to begin and end, what to include, and how to connect events into a meaningful sequence. The theorist Hayden White pressed the point provocatively, arguing that historical writing borrows the devices of literature — plot, emphasis, characterisation — so that the shape of a history is partly a rhetorical and imaginative construction, not simply given by the facts. Most historians accept that narrative involves choices while insisting that those choices remain disciplined by evidence.

Interpretation, then, is neither free invention nor mechanical deduction. It is a reasoned, evidence-bound argument about what the sources mean, why events unfolded as they did, and how they connect. Two historians may interpret the same evidence differently and both be defensible, yet not all interpretations are equal: the better one accounts more fully and honestly for the evidence, acknowledges complexity, and withstands criticism. This is the demanding, irreducibly interpretive core of the historian's craft.

sections.heading: Bias, Silence, and Contested History
sections.body:
History is written by people, and people bring perspectives, assumptions, and limits to their work, so the question of bias is unavoidable and must be faced honestly rather than wished away. Bias enters at every stage: in the sources themselves, which were made by particular people with their own interests; in the survival of evidence, since what happens to be preserved is not a neutral sample of the past; in the questions historians choose to ask; and in the interpretations they reach. A mature understanding of history recognises these influences and treats them as objects of analysis rather than as fatal flaws that make all history mere opinion.

The uneven survival and creation of sources produces what the anthropologist and historian Michel-Rolph Trouillot called silences: the systematic absence from the record of certain people and events. The powerful generate and preserve records; the powerless often do not, and their experiences can be silenced at the moment of the event, in the making of archives, and in the writing of history. Recognising these silences — asking who is missing and why — is essential to avoid mistaking the surviving record for the whole of the past, and it has driven much recent effort to recover the histories of women, enslaved and colonised peoples, and the poor.

A related pitfall is presentism, the tendency to judge and interpret the past by the values and knowledge of the present, or to read the past as merely leading up to our own time. The historian Herbert Butterfield criticised this as the Whig interpretation of history, which treats the past as a story of progress toward present arrangements, distorting it by praising those who seem to anticipate us and condemning those who do not. Guarding against presentism means striving to understand past people in their own terms and context, though historians debate how far this is possible or even desirable, since every historian inevitably works from a present standpoint.

Because history bears on identity, politics, and power, it is often contested, and here a vital distinction must be drawn between legitimate revisionism and denial. Revisionism, the continual reinterpretation of the past in light of new evidence and new questions, is the normal, healthy operation of the discipline; the historical understanding of almost every major topic has rightly changed over time. Denialism, by contrast — such as the denial of well-documented atrocities like the Holocaust — is not legitimate history but the rejection or falsification of overwhelming evidence for ideological ends. The difference lies in method: genuine revisionism argues from evidence and submits to scholarly criticism, while denial ignores or fabricates evidence and immunises itself against refutation.

Historians therefore do not claim a false neutrality, but they do commit to intellectual honesty: acknowledging their standpoint, following the evidence even when it is uncomfortable, representing sources fairly, and exposing their reasoning to challenge. Objectivity in history is best understood not as the absence of perspective but as a disciplined, self-aware, evidence-bound practice that keeps bias in check and remains open to correction.

sections.heading: Schools of Thought and the Future of the Discipline
sections.body:
The methods described in this guide did not appear all at once; they developed through competing schools of thought, each emphasising different questions, sources, and ways of explaining the past. Understanding these traditions helps a reader see that there is no single fixed way to do history, but rather an evolving conversation. The nineteenth-century professionalisation of history under Ranke and his followers established the ideal of rigorous, document-based political and diplomatic history, focused on states, rulers, and events, and grounded in archival research.

In the twentieth century, powerful reactions broadened the field. The French Annales school, led by Marc Bloch, Lucien Febvre, and later Fernand Braudel, turned from the history of events and great men toward the deep structures of ordinary life — geography, climate, economy, technology, and collective mental worlds — and introduced the idea of the longue durée, the study of slow-moving, long-term change beneath the surface of events. Marxist historians emphasised economic forces and class conflict as engines of change, directing attention to labour, production, and the experience of ordinary working people. The social history that flourished from the mid-century, and the history from below discussed earlier, extended the cast of history to the whole of society.

Later movements pushed further. The cultural turn and the influence of anthropology led historians to study meaning, symbols, rituals, and mentalities, asking how past people understood their world. Gender history and women's history recovered half the human past long neglected, and showed how ideas of masculinity and femininity shaped every society. Global and transnational history reacted against the older focus on single nations, tracing connections, exchanges, and comparisons across the world and challenging Europe-centred narratives. Quantitative history, or cliometrics, applied statistical methods to large bodies of data such as prices, populations, and trade, while environmental history placed human affairs within the history of the natural world.

Today the discipline is being reshaped again by digital tools. The digitisation of archives, the searching of vast text corpora, mapping with geographic information systems, network analysis, and the statistical study of large datasets are opening questions that could not previously be asked, even as they raise new problems of method and interpretation. At the same time, the enduring debates — between structure and agency, between narrative and analysis, between objectivity and perspective — remain very much alive.

What unites this diversity is the shared commitment described throughout this guide: to reconstruct the past from evidence, tested critically and interpreted honestly. History connects outward to nearly every other field, drawing on the sciences for dating and analysis, on the social sciences for models of human behaviour, and on literature and philosophy for the arts of narrative and interpretation. For the reader, the deepest lesson is that history is not a fixed body of facts to be memorised but a living method of inquiry — a disciplined, self-critical, endlessly revisable way of asking what happened, why, and how we can know.

guides.title: The Philosophy of History
guides.summary: What philosophers have claimed about the shape and meaning of the human past, and what they have concluded about how historical knowledge is possible at all — from cyclical antiquity and providential Christianity through Hegel, Marx and Ranke to narrative theory, causation and the limits of objectivity.

sections.heading: Two Different Questions Hiding Under One Name
sections.body:
The philosophy of history is not one subject but two, and a great deal of confusion follows from failing to separate them. The first, traditionally called speculative or substantive philosophy of history, asks about the past itself: does history as a whole have a shape, a direction, a mechanism or a meaning? Is it cyclical, linear, progressive, providential, or merely one damned thing after another? The second, called critical or analytic philosophy of history, asks about historical knowledge: what is a historical explanation, how do we justify claims about events no one now living observed, what role does narrative play, and can a historian be objective?

The two questions are logically independent. A person can believe that history has no overall pattern and still hold sophisticated views about how historians establish causes. Conversely, one can hold that history is driven by economic forces while being naive about evidence. In practice the two have been intertwined, because grand theories about the shape of the past almost always smuggle in assumptions about what counts as significant, and methodological choices about what to study almost always presuppose some view of what matters.

The subject earns its place for reasons that are not merely academic. Every political programme that appeals to the direction of history — the inevitability of a revolution, the arc of moral progress, the return to a lost golden age, the clash of civilisations — is making a substantive philosophical claim about the past, usually without acknowledging it and usually without argument. Every dispute about how a country should teach its history is a dispute about objectivity, selection and moral judgement. The tools for assessing such claims are exactly the tools this field has developed.

The term itself is comparatively recent. Voltaire coined philosophie de l'histoire around 1765 to describe a way of writing about the past that looked for the development of customs, arts and commerce rather than reciting the deeds of kings and the interventions of Providence. But the underlying questions are much older, and they were posed with considerable sophistication in ancient Greece and Rome, in classical China, in the Islamic world and in medieval Christendom long before the label existed.

One preliminary distinction is worth fixing. The word history is systematically ambiguous between the events themselves — what the Germans call Geschehen, what happened — and the account of them, Historie or Geschichtsschreibung, what is written. Much apparent disagreement in this field turns on which is meant. The claim that history is a construction is trivially true of the second and highly contentious about the first, and writers have exploited that ambiguity, sometimes deliberately. A third sense is worth adding: history also names the academic discipline with its training, journals and standards. Confusing the discipline with the past it studies produces the lazy objection that history is merely what the winners wrote, which is a claim about the sociology of the profession, not an argument about whether particular events occurred.

sections.heading: Antiquity: Inquiry, Cycles and the Instructive Past
sections.body:
The Greeks invented history as a genre and, almost immediately, began arguing about what it was for. Herodotus, writing in the mid-fifth century BCE, opens his Histories by describing his work as an inquiry — historiē, meaning investigation — intended to preserve great deeds from oblivion and to explain why Greeks and Persians came to fight. His method is capacious: he reports rival versions, distinguishes what he saw from what he was told, and includes ethnography, geography and marvels. His explanatory frame is partly moral and partly religious: excessive prosperity attracts divine resentment, and hubris invites nemesis.

Thucydides, a generation later, is deliberately narrower and more austere. He restricts himself to contemporary political and military affairs, excludes the divine as an explanatory factor, subjects testimony to cross-examination, and states his purpose explicitly: because human nature remains constant, events resembling those he describes will recur, and his work is therefore a possession for all time rather than a prize essay for immediate hearing. This is the first clear statement of a recurrent idea — that history yields transferable knowledge because the underlying human material does not change.

Cyclical thinking was the dominant substantive framework. Polybius, writing in the second century BCE, gave it its most systematic classical form in the sixth book of his Histories, with the doctrine of anacyclosis: constitutions degenerate in a predictable sequence, monarchy into tyranny, aristocracy into oligarchy, democracy into mob rule, whereupon the cycle begins again. Rome's stability, he argued, came from its mixed constitution, which balanced the three pure forms and slowed the rotation. Here is a genuine theoretical model with a mechanism and a prediction.

Chinese historiography developed independently and reached comparable sophistication. Sima Qian, completing the Shiji around 91 BCE, organised the past into annals, tables, treatises and biographies, and worked within an interpretive tradition in which dynasties rise and fall according to the Mandate of Heaven — a scheme that is cyclical in form but strongly moral in content, since loss of virtue precedes loss of legitimacy.

What antiquity largely lacked was the idea of cumulative progress. The past was a repertoire of examples, a stock of exemplary and cautionary cases from which statesmen and generals could learn, and the assumption that the future would resemble it is precisely what made it instructive. Roman writers such as Livy and Tacitus wrote in a register of decline from ancestral virtue. The notion that the human condition might be permanently and progressively transformed by accumulated knowledge would have struck most classical authors as implausible. Two further legacies of the classical inheritance deserve notice. The first is the appeal to exemplary lives, developed most fully by Plutarch, in which biography carries moral instruction and the past functions as a gallery of characters to imitate or avoid. The second is the persistent tension between fortune and virtue, between what agents control and what merely happens to them, which supplies the basic dramatic structure of ancient historiography and never entirely leaves the tradition.

sections.heading: Augustine and the Invention of Linear, Meaningful Time
sections.body:
Christianity introduced into Western thought a conception of history that was linear, unrepeatable, universal and directed toward an end, and this was a genuine intellectual innovation whose consequences reach far beyond theology. If the world was created at a definite moment, if the Incarnation happened once and cannot recur, and if history will terminate in a Last Judgement, then time is not a wheel but an arrow, and every event has a unique and unrepeatable position within a single story that includes all of humanity.

Augustine of Hippo gave this framework its classic formulation in The City of God, written between roughly 413 and 426 CE in response to the sack of Rome by Alaric in 410 and the pagan accusation that abandoning the old gods had brought catastrophe. Augustine's answer was to deny that earthly political fortune measures divine favour at all. Two cities, distinguished by the objects of their love — the earthly city by love of self, the heavenly by love of God — are intermingled throughout history and will be separated only at its end. Rome's fall is therefore theologically uninformative. Empires rise and fall; the sacred narrative runs underneath and through them, invisible to political analysis.

Several features of this scheme proved extraordinarily durable, surviving the loss of the theology that generated them. The first is universality: history is the history of humanity as a whole, not of one city or people. The second is periodisation into meaningful epochs rather than mere sequence. The third, and most consequential, is teleology: the past is intelligible because it is going somewhere, and events acquire significance from their place in a trajectory rather than from their intrinsic scale.

The medieval elaboration ran in several directions. Orosius produced a universal chronicle at Augustine's prompting; Otto of Freising in the twelfth century wrote a history structured on the two cities. More radical was Joachim of Fiore, who around 1200 divided history into three ages corresponding to Father, Son and Holy Spirit, with the third — an age of spiritual freedom — imminent. Joachim's tripartite scheme, with its promise of a coming transformed condition within history rather than after it, has been argued by scholars such as Karl Löwith and Eric Voegelin to be the ancestor of later secular theories of progress and revolution.

That argument, the so-called secularisation thesis, remains contested. Hans Blumenberg replied that modernity's idea of progress is a genuine achievement rather than a transposed eschatology. The dispute matters because it asks whether the confident modern claim that history has a direction is an argued conclusion or an inherited habit. Whatever the verdict, the practical effects of the Christian scheme were durable. It made universal chronology a scholarly problem, prompting centuries of effort to synchronise biblical, Greek, Roman and Near Eastern dating into a single timeline. It established the convention of counting years from a fixed point, adopted from Dionysius Exiguus in the sixth century and diffused widely by Bede. And it made the idea of a single human story, rather than many unrelated ones, seem natural.

sections.heading: Ibn Khaldun and the First Science of Society
sections.body:
The most original work of historical theory produced anywhere before the eighteenth century was written in North Africa in 1377. Ibn Khaldun, a Tunisian-born jurist, diplomat and scholar who lived from 1332 to 1406, composed the Muqaddimah as the introduction to a universal history, and used it to propose something no previous historian had attempted: a distinct science whose object is human social organisation itself, which he called ilm al-umran, the science of civilisation.

His starting point is a methodological complaint. Historians, he argues, uncritically transmit absurdities — impossible army sizes, fantastical genealogies, physically impossible events — because they assess reports only by the reliability of the chain of transmitters rather than by whether the reported event is compatible with how societies actually work. His remedy is to establish the general laws of social life first, and then to use them as a standard against which particular reports can be tested. This is a startlingly modern proposal: a theory of society functioning as a criterion of source criticism.

The central concept is asabiyyah, usually rendered as group feeling, social cohesion or solidarity. It is strongest in harsh environments where survival demands mutual dependence, and it is the resource that allows a group to conquer and found a dynasty. But conquest brings cities, wealth, luxury, taxation, specialised administration and hired soldiers, and each of these erodes the solidarity that made conquest possible. Ibn Khaldun sketches the resulting arc across roughly four generations — a builder, a consolidator, an imitator and a squanderer — giving dynasties a characteristic lifespan he estimates at around one hundred and twenty years, after which a fresh group with intact asabiyyah replaces them.

Around this he assembles observations of remarkable acuity: that a city's economy depends on the density and division of its labour; that excessive taxation eventually reduces total revenue by destroying the incentive to produce, an argument anticipating much later fiscal theory; that climate and diet shape ways of life; that the conquered tend to imitate the culture of their conquerors.

Two cautions are worth registering. Ibn Khaldun's model was drawn from the specific dynamics of the Maghreb, where nomadic tribal confederations repeatedly overturned settled dynasties, and it generalises less well elsewhere. And his cycle is not progressive: civilisation rises, decays and is renewed by outsiders, with no cumulative direction. Nevertheless the Muqaddimah stands alone. It had limited influence in Europe until translations appeared in the nineteenth century, by which time comparable ideas had been developed independently, which is itself a useful reminder that intellectual history is not a single relay race. His methodological insistence is the part that has aged best. To test a report against what we know of how societies function, rather than against the reputation of whoever transmitted it, is precisely the move that separates critical history from chronicle. Modern historians who reject an implausible casualty figure because it exceeds what the region's agriculture could have fed are doing exactly what Ibn Khaldun prescribed six centuries earlier.

sections.heading: Vico: We Can Know History Because We Made It
sections.body:
Giambattista Vico, a poorly paid professor of rhetoric in Naples who lived from 1668 to 1744, produced in the successive editions of his New Science, published in 1725, 1730 and 1744, an argument that has shaped the philosophy of history ever since, though it was almost entirely ignored in his lifetime.

His central principle is compressed into a Latin formula: verum ipsum factum, the true is precisely the made. We can have genuine knowledge only of what we ourselves have constructed. On this criterion, Vico turns the prestige ranking of his age upside down. Nature was made by God, so only God knows it fully; human beings can describe regularities in it but cannot grasp it from the inside. The world of nations — laws, languages, customs, institutions, myths — was made by human beings, and therefore is in principle knowable with a certainty the natural sciences cannot attain. This is a direct rebuke to Descartes, who had dismissed history as an unreliable branch of learning fit only for polite conversation.

The method Vico builds on this is essentially imaginative reconstruction. To understand an early society one must recover its mentality, which he insists is genuinely alien: the earliest humans were not defective philosophers but poets, thinking in what he called poetic wisdom, through vivid concrete images and personifications rather than abstractions. Myth is therefore not a lie or a confusion but the authentic record of how such minds understood their world, and it can be decoded. Etymology and the comparative study of laws and customs become historical evidence of the first rank.

Vico's substantive scheme divides the history of every nation into three ages — of gods, of heroes, and of men — each with its own characteristic language, jurisprudence, form of authority and mode of thought. Nations pass through them in order, reach a peak of rational refinement, and then decay into what he memorably called the barbarism of reflection, a condition more destructive than primitive barbarism because it dissolves the shared beliefs that hold a people together. Society then collapses and the cycle recommences at a higher level, a movement he called corsi e ricorsi.

The lasting contribution is not the three ages, which few now defend, but the epistemological turn. Vico established that the past is a foreign country whose inhabitants thought differently, that this difference is recoverable through evidence rather than assumed away, and that historical understanding is a distinct kind of knowing. Every later argument about interpretation, empathy and cultural relativism descends from this. His reception illustrates a recurring feature of the field. Ignored in his lifetime and unread for a century, Vico was rediscovered by Michelet in the 1820s, admired by Marx, taken up by Croce and Collingwood, and made central again by Isaiah Berlin in the twentieth century. Ideas in the philosophy of history do not simply accumulate; they lie dormant and are recovered when a later generation finds a use for them.

sections.heading: The Enlightenment and the Idea of Progress
sections.body:
The eighteenth century produced the substantive philosophy of history that has proved most influential in ordinary life: the belief that history has a direction, that the direction is broadly upward, and that the engine is the growth and diffusion of knowledge.

Voltaire's Essay on the Customs and Spirit of the Nations, published in 1756, is the manifesto. He deliberately displaces battles and dynasties in favour of commerce, arts, manners and opinion; he includes China, India and the Islamic world rather than treating European Christendom as the whole story; and he removes Providence as an explanatory principle, substituting human folly, superstition and, occasionally, reason. History becomes a secular study of civilisation rather than a record of divine management.

Turgot, in lectures delivered at the Sorbonne in 1750, supplied the mechanism. Nature repeats itself; humanity does not, because language and writing allow each generation to inherit what previous ones discovered. Knowledge is cumulative, and cumulative knowledge transforms the conditions of life irreversibly. Condorcet pushed this to its limit in his Sketch for a Historical Picture of the Progress of the Human Mind, written in 1793 and 1794 while he was in hiding from the Terror that would shortly kill him, and published posthumously in 1795. He divides history into ten stages, the tenth still to come, and predicts the abolition of inequality between nations and classes, the equality of women, the spread of education, and the indefinite extension of the human lifespan. The circumstances of its composition make it either the most admirable or the most deluded document in the tradition, and reasonable readers differ.

Kant's short essay of 1784, Idea for a Universal History with a Cosmopolitan Purpose, is the philosophically sharpest treatment. He concedes that individual human actions appear chaotic, yet notes that aggregate statistics such as marriages and births are remarkably regular, and proposes that we may read history as if it followed a hidden plan of nature. His mechanism is antagonism — what he calls unsocial sociability, the human need for company combined with the equal need to dominate it. Competition drives the development of talents, which requires law, which requires a just civil constitution, which is impossible in isolation and therefore ultimately requires a lawful federation of states. Progress is not guaranteed; it is a regulative idea we are entitled to adopt because acting on it makes it more likely.

Adam Smith, John Millar and the Scottish school added the influential four-stages theory, in which societies progress from hunting through pastoralism and agriculture to commerce, with property forms and legal institutions following the mode of subsistence — a materialist scheme that anticipates much of the nineteenth century. It is worth registering how much the confident version of this outlook owed to circumstance. The optimism of Turgot and Condorcet was formed in a century of rising European wealth, expanding literacy and spectacular success in the physical sciences, and it generalised from that experience to humanity as a whole. Later readers have found it hard to separate the defensible claim, that knowledge accumulates, from the far stronger one, that moral and political improvement follows automatically.

sections.heading: Herder and the Counter-Enlightenment: Every Age Is Its Own
sections.body:
Against the confident universalism of the philosophes, a German reaction insisted that the Enlightenment's yardstick was parochial. Johann Gottfried Herder, who lived from 1744 to 1803, launched it in 1774 with a polemic whose title translates roughly as Yet Another Philosophy of History, and developed it more soberly in his Ideas for the Philosophy of the History of Mankind between 1784 and 1791.

His objection is that judging past ages by whether they approximate to eighteenth-century Paris is an error of the same kind as judging a child by whether it can do a man's work. Every people and every period possesses its own centre of gravity, its own standard of happiness, its own way of being human, shaped by climate, language, tradition and geography. The Middle Ages are not a failed attempt at modernity but a different and internally coherent form of life. Herder's slogan, in Ranke's later formulation of the same intuition, is that every epoch is immediate to God — valuable in itself, not as a rung on a ladder.

Language is central to his argument. Because thought is inseparable from the particular language in which it is conducted, and because languages differ in structure and vocabulary, peoples genuinely think differently. A culture is therefore an organic whole whose parts — poetry, law, religion, custom — express a single formative spirit, and understanding it requires entering into it, not measuring it. Herder collected folk songs precisely because he regarded them as the authentic voice of a people rather than as crude versions of literary poetry.

This position is historicism in its original and best sense: the doctrine that human phenomena can only be understood historically, as the product of a particular development, and that there are no timeless standards standing outside history by which to rank them. Its intellectual dividends were enormous. It underwrote comparative philology, the study of folklore, cultural anthropology, and the whole methodological insistence that the historian must reconstruct a period's own categories rather than impose modern ones.

Its costs were also real, and Herder is not fairly blamed for all of them. Once a people is conceived as an organic unity with a distinctive spirit, the step to nineteenth-century ethnic nationalism is short, though Herder himself was cosmopolitan, opposed to conquest and hostile to claims of national superiority. More philosophically, thoroughgoing historicism threatens to undercut itself: if all standards are products of their age, that judgement is a product of its own age too, and there is no stable ground from which to condemn any past practice. This relativist difficulty has never been fully resolved, and it recurs in every subsequent generation of the debate. Herder also bequeathed a working method rather than merely a doctrine. If a period must be understood in its own terms, then the historian's first task is to recover its vocabulary, its assumptions about nature and authority, and the questions it thought worth asking. That programme underwrites everything from the history of mentalities to modern conceptual history, and it is the reason serious historians now treat anachronism as a technical error rather than a stylistic lapse.

sections.heading: Hegel: World History as the Progress of the Consciousness of Freedom
sections.body:
Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, who lived from 1770 to 1831, produced the most ambitious substantive philosophy of history ever attempted. His lectures on the subject, delivered repeatedly in Berlin between 1822 and 1831 and published posthumously in 1837, open by rejecting the view that reason is something the historian brings to a chaotic past. Reason, he claims, is in history; the task is to exhibit it.

The subject of history for Hegel is Geist — spirit, or mind, understood not as an individual psychology but as the collective, objective, self-developing rationality embodied in a people's laws, art, religion and institutions. Its content is freedom, and the famous formula is that world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom. He periodises accordingly: in the ancient Oriental world, one is free, namely the despot; in the Greek and Roman world, some are free, resting on slavery; in the Germanic-Christian world, in principle all are free, because Christianity introduced the idea of the infinite worth of every individual soul and modern institutions gradually made it actual.

The motor is dialectical. A form of social life develops its own internal contradictions, which drive it toward a successor that resolves them while preserving what was rational in it — the process Hegel calls Aufhebung, a term meaning simultaneously to cancel, to preserve and to raise up. The Greek city-state, for instance, achieved a beautiful unity of citizen and community but could not accommodate the claims of individual conscience, a tension Hegel reads in the trial of Socrates and in the Antigone, and which ultimately dissolved it.

Two doctrines cause the most trouble and the most interest. The cunning of reason holds that individuals pursue their private passions and interests, and that the larger rational outcome is produced through them without being intended by anyone; Hegel calls world-historical individuals, such as Caesar or Napoleon, those whose personal aims happen to coincide with what the next stage requires. And his notorious statement that history is a slaughter-bench on which the happiness of peoples and the virtue of individuals are sacrificed acknowledges the cost without treating it as a refutation.

The objections are formidable and were made immediately. The scheme is teleological in a way that permits retrospective justification of anything that succeeded. Its evidence is highly selective and its treatment of Africa, India and China dismissive to the point of prejudice. It is unfalsifiable, since any development can be redescribed as a moment of the dialectic. Yet its indirect influence is inescapable: the vocabulary of contradiction, historical stages, alienation and the eventual reconciliation of the individual and the community structures nearly all subsequent debate. It is also worth separating Hegel's method from his conclusions. The insight that institutions can generate the very tensions that destroy them, that an arrangement can be rational for a period and then become an obstacle, and that historical actors typically do not understand the significance of what they are doing, all survive detachment from the metaphysics of Spirit. Many historians who would reject every word of Hegel's system nonetheless reason in exactly these terms.

sections.heading: Marx and Historical Materialism
sections.body:
Karl Marx, who lived from 1818 to 1883, took Hegel's dialectical structure and, in his own phrase, set it on its feet: instead of consciousness determining social being, social being determines consciousness. The result, historical materialism, is the most consequential substantive philosophy of history of the modern era, whatever one concludes about its validity.

The most compact statement is the 1859 preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy. In the social production of their existence, people enter into relations of production appropriate to a given stage of the productive forces; the sum of these relations constitutes the economic structure, the real foundation on which arises a legal and political superstructure and to which correspond definite forms of social consciousness. At a certain stage the developing productive forces come into conflict with the existing relations of production, which turn from forms of development into fetters, and an epoch of social revolution begins.

The scheme yields a succession of modes of production — Marx variously names primitive communal, ancient slave, feudal, capitalist, with a projected socialist successor — each with its characteristic class structure and its characteristic contradiction. Class struggle is the mechanism by which transitions occur. The theory is explanatory rather than merely descriptive: it claims to say why feudalism gave way to capitalism, and it locates the answer in the incompatibility between new productive techniques and old juridical and social forms.

Marx is more careful than his popularisers about determinism. The Eighteenth Brumaire of 1852 begins by observing that people make their own history, but not of their own free will, and not under circumstances they have chosen. His late letters and Engels's correspondence insist that the economic factor is determining only in the last instance and that politics, law and ideology exert reciprocal influence. Whether this qualification can be made precise without draining the theory of content is a live question.

Criticism has run along several lines. Empirically, the predicted immiseration of the proletariat and the revolutions in the most advanced capitalist economies did not occur; revolutions came instead in agrarian societies. Methodologically, Karl Popper argued that the theory was repeatedly rescued by auxiliary hypotheses and thereby rendered unfalsifiable. Analytically, G. A. Cohen's reconstruction in 1978 defended a functional reading, arguing that relations of production persist because they promote the development of productive forces — a defence which itself provoked debate about whether functional explanation is legitimate.

What survives independently of the political programme is durable: the insistence that material conditions, technology, class and property shape thought and institutions, and that ideas are worth investigating for the interests they serve. Marxism's deeper effect on the discipline was to change what counted as a historical subject. Wages, harvests, land tenure, guild regulations, strikes and household budgets became evidence about the shape of a society rather than background detail. The social history of the mid-twentieth century, much of it written by people who were not Marxists and some by people who were hostile to Marxism, is unimaginable without that shift in attention.

sections.heading: Ranke and the Professionalisation of History as a Discipline
sections.body:
While philosophers were constructing systems, a parallel revolution was making history into a research profession with methods, training and institutional standards. Its emblem is Leopold von Ranke, who lived from 1795 to 1886 and taught at Berlin for nearly half a century.

The famous phrase comes from the preface to his first book in 1824: history has been assigned the office of judging the past and instructing the present for the benefit of future ages, but the present attempt does not aspire to such high offices; it wants only to show what actually happened — wie es eigentlich gewesen. The sentence has been misread for a century as a claim to naive factual positivism. Ranke's German word eigentlich carried in his usage a sense closer to essentially or characteristically, and he was a devout Lutheran who believed each period expressed a divine idea. His point was against moralising and against subordinating the past to present purposes, not a denial that interpretation is required.

The methodological substance is what mattered. Ranke insisted on primary sources — state archives, diplomatic dispatches, private correspondence — over the compilations and chronicles historians had traditionally recycled. He formalised techniques of source criticism inherited from classical philology and from earlier scholars such as the Benedictine Jean Mabillon, who in 1681 had established rules for detecting forged charters. External criticism establishes a document's authenticity, date and provenance; internal criticism assesses the author's position, purpose, access to information and bias. Where sources conflict, one prefers the earlier, the closer to the event, the disinterested, and the corroborated.

Equally important was the seminar. Ranke's Berlin seminar trained students by having them collectively dissect documents, and this model, exported worldwide, created a self-policing scholarly community in which claims must be footnoted, evidence must be citable and findings must survive criticism by specialists. History acquired the social apparatus of a science even where it lacked the logical apparatus.

The professional turn had costs. Archival preference privileged states, diplomacy and elites, because those are the institutions that generate and preserve records, and it correspondingly marginalised the illiterate, the poor, women, the colonised and the enslaved. Twentieth-century movements — the Annales school founded by Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre in 1929, social history, history from below, microhistory — were substantially reactions against this bias, widening the evidential base to include parish registers, tax rolls, court depositions, wills, price series, pollen and grain records. Fernand Braudel's distinction between the almost motionless time of geography, the slow rhythms of social structures, and the surface agitation of events remains one of the most useful analytical tools the discipline has produced. The professionalisation also created a durable tension that is not resolvable in principle. The techniques that make history reliable — footnotes, archives, specialist languages, peer review — also make it slow, narrow and largely unreadable outside the academy, while the sweeping accounts that reach a wide public are usually the least rigorous. Every generation restages this argument between the monograph and the grand narrative, and neither side has ever fully won.

sections.heading: Understanding versus Explaining: Dilthey, Windelband and Weber
sections.body:
A specifically German debate in the late nineteenth century framed a question the field has never escaped: is history a science of the same type as physics, or a fundamentally different kind of enquiry?

Wilhelm Dilthey, who lived from 1833 to 1911, argued for a fundamental division between the natural sciences and what he called the Geisteswissenschaften, the human or moral sciences. Nature is external to us and can only be explained by subsuming events under general laws — Erklären. Human life is something we live from the inside, and its products can therefore be understood — Verstehen — by re-experiencing the mental life expressed in them. The historian works within a hermeneutic circle: the meaning of any part of a text or a life depends on the whole, while the whole is accessible only through its parts, so interpretation proceeds by successive refinement rather than by deduction.

Wilhelm Windelband, in a rectoral address of 1894, proposed a different cut. The distinction is not between subject matters but between aims. Nomothetic enquiry seeks general laws; idiographic enquiry seeks to characterise the particular in its uniqueness. Any subject can be approached either way. Heinrich Rickert developed this into a theory of value-relevance: the infinite manifold of past reality must be selected from, and selection is guided by relation to values a culture regards as significant, which is not the same as the historian making value judgements.

Max Weber, who lived from 1864 to 1920, produced the most usable synthesis. He accepted value-relevance in the choice of problems while insisting on value-freedom in their treatment: what you study is inevitably shaped by what your society cares about, but once you are studying it your conclusions must not be bent to your preferences. He introduced the ideal type — a deliberately one-sided conceptual construct, such as bureaucracy or the Protestant ethic, which no case matches exactly but against which real cases can be measured. And he offered a treatment of historical causation, borrowed from the jurist Johannes von Kries, that remains the best available: to say that a factor caused an outcome is to say that had it been absent, the outcome would have been significantly less probable, judged against our general knowledge of how such situations develop. This makes counterfactual reasoning explicit and disciplined rather than idle.

Weber's answer to the founding question is therefore both and neither.
